We note that recently, many studies design algorithms or systems by jointly considering different types of methods so that a method can enjoy the merits of both sides (Lu et al., 2021; Zhao et al., 2023; Chen et al., 2018; Japan, 2022; Aguerrebere et al., 2023; Chen et al., 2023; Douze et al., 2018). Our work proposes a quantization method which provides a sharp error bound and good empirical performance at the same time. Just like the conventional quantization methods, it can work as a component in an integrated algorithm or system. Our method has two additional advantages: (1) it involves no parameter tuning and (2) it supports efficient distance estimation for a single quantization code. These advantages may further smoothen its combination with other types of methods. Recently, there are a thread of methods which apply machine learning (ML) on ANN (Baranchuk et al., 2019; Feng et al., 2022; Li et al., 2020; Dong et al., 2020; Li et al., 2023; Wang et al., 2022; Xiao et al., 2022).

Quantization. There is a vast literature about the quantization of high-dimensional vectors from different communities including machine learning, computer vision and data management (Jegou et al., 2010; Babenko and Lempitsky, 2014; Gong et al., 2013; Paparrizos et al., 2022; Zhang et al., 2014; Ge et al., 2013; Martinez et al., 2016; Martinez et al., 2018; Ferhatosmanoglu et al., 2000; Tuncel et al., 2002; Weber et al., 1998). We refer readers to comprehensive surveys (Wang et al., 2016; Wang et al., 2018; Matsui et al., 2018; Echihabi et al., 2018) and reference books (Zezula et al., 2010; Samet, 2005). It is worth of mentioning that in (Tuncel et al., 2002), a quantization method called Split-VQ was mentioned. The method covers the major idea of PQ, i.e., it splits the vectors into sub-segments, constructs sub-codebooks for each sub-segment and forms the codebook with Cartesian product. Besides PQ and its variants, there are other types of quantization methods, e.g., scalar quantization (Aguerrebere et al., 2023; Ferhatosmanoglu et al., 2000; Weber et al., 1998). These methods quantize the scalar values of each dimension separately, which often adopt more moderate compression rates than PQ in exchange for better accuracy. In particular, VA+ File (Ferhatosmanoglu et al., 2000), a scalar quantization method, has shown leading performance on the similarity search of data series according to a recent benchmark (Echihabi et al., 2018). Besides the studies on the quantization algorithms, we note that hardware-aware optimization (with SIMD, GPU, FPGA, etc) also makes significant contributions to the performance of these methods (André et al., 2015; André et al., 2017; Jiang et al., 2023; Liu et al., 2023; Johnson et al., 2019). To inherit the merits of the well-developed hardware-aware optimization, in this work, we reduce our computation to the computation of PQ (Section 3.3). However, RaBitQ, in its nature, can be implemented with much simpler bitwise operations (which is not possible for PQ and its variants). It remains to be an interesting question whether dedicated hardware-aware optimization can further improve the performance of RaBitQ.

Theoretical Studies on High-Dimensional Vectors. The theoretical studies on high-dimensional vectors are primarily about the seminal Johnson-Lindenstrauss (JL) Lemma (Johnson and Lindenstrauss, 1984). It presents that reducing the dimensionality of a vector to O⁡(ϵ−2​log⁡(1/δ))O(\epsilon^{-2}\log(1/\delta)) suffices to guarantee the error bound of ϵ\epsilon. Recent advances improve the JL Lemma in different aspects. For example, (Larsen and Nelson, 2017) proves the optimality of the JL Lemma. (Ailon and Chazelle, 2009; Kane and Nelson, 2014) propose fast algorithms to do the dimension reduction. We refer readers to a comprehensive survey (Freksen, 2021). Our method fits into a recent line of studies (Alon and Klartag, 2017; Indyk and Wagner, 2022; Pagh and Sivertsen, 2020; Indyk et al., 2017), which target to improve the JL Lemma by compressing high-dimensional vectors into short codes. As a comparison, to guarantee an error bound of ϵ\epsilon, the JL Lemma requires a vector of O⁡(ϵ−2​log⁡(1/δ))O(\epsilon^{-2}\log(1/\delta)) dimensions while these studies prove that a short code with O⁡(ϵ−2​log⁡(1/δ))O(\epsilon^{-2}\log(1/\delta)) bits would be sufficient. In practical terms, we note that although the existing studies achieve the improvement in theory in terms of the space complexity (i.e., the minimum number of bits needed for guaranteeing a certain error bound), they care less about the improvement in efficiency. In particular, these methods do not suit the in-memory ANN search because, for estimating the distance during the query phase, they need decompress the short codes and compute the distances with the decompressed vectors, which degrades to the brute force in efficiency. For this reason, these methods have not been adopted in practice. In contrast, our method supports practically efficient computation as is specified in Section 3.3.

Signed Random Projection. We note that there are a line of studies named signed random projection (SRP) which generate a short code for estimating the angular values between vectors via binarizing the vectors after randomization (Charikar, 2002; Kang and Wong, 2018; Dubey et al., 2022; Ji et al., 2012). We note that our method is different from these studies in the following aspects. (1) Problem-wise, SRP targets to unbiasedly estimate the angular value while RaBitQ targets to unbiasedly estimate the inner product (and further, the squared distances). Note that the relationship between the angular value and the inner product is non-linear. The unbiased estimator for one does not trivially derive an unbiased estimator for the other. (2) Theory-wise, RaBitQ has a stronger type of guarantee than SRP. In particular, RaBitQ guarantees that every data vector has its distance within the bounds with high probability. In contrast, SRP only bounds the variance, i.e., the “average” squared error, and it does not provide a bound for every estimated value. Thus, it cannot help with the re-ranking in similarity search. (3) Technique-wise, in SRP the bit strings are viewed as some hashing codes while in RaBitQ, the bit strings are the binary representations of bi-valued vectors. Moreover, SRP maps both the data and query vectors to bit strings, which introduces error from both sides. In contrast, RaBitQ quantizes the data vectors to be bit strings and the query vectors to be vectors of 4-bit unsigned integers. Theorem 3.3 proves that quantizing the query vectors only introduces negligible error. Thus, RaBitQ only introduces the error from the side of the data vector.

7. conclusion

In conclusion, we propose a novel randomized quantization method RaBitQ which has clear advantages in both empirical accuracy and rigorous theoretical error bound over PQ and its variants. The proposed efficient implementations based on simple bitwise operations or fast SIMD-based operations further make it stand out in terms of the time-accuracy trade-off for the in-memory ANN search. Extensive experiments on real-world datasets verify both (1) the empirical superiority of our method in terms of the time-accuracy trade-off and (2) the alignment of the empirical performance with the theoretical analysis. Some interesting research directions include applying our method in other scenarios of ANN search (e.g., with graph-based indexes or on other storage devices (Jayaram Subramanya et al., 2019; Chen et al., 2021; Liu et al., 2017; Jang et al., 2023)). Besides, RaBitQ can also be trivially applied to unbiasedly estimate cosine similarity and inner product 88 8 The cosine similarity of two vectors exactly equals to the inner product of their unit vectors. The inner product of 𝐨\mathbf{o} and 𝐪\mathbf{q} can be expressed as ⟨𝐨,𝐪⟩=⟨𝐨−𝐜+𝐜,𝐪−𝐜+𝐜⟩=‖𝐨−𝐜‖⋅‖𝐪−𝐜‖⋅⟨(𝐨−𝐜)/‖𝐨−𝐜‖,(𝐪−𝐜)/‖𝐪−𝐜‖⟩+⟨𝐨,𝐜⟩+⟨𝐪,𝐜⟩−‖𝐜‖2\left<\mathbf{o},\mathbf{q}\right>=\left<\mathbf{o-c+c},\mathbf{q-c+c}\right>=\|\mathbf{o-c}\|\cdot\|\mathbf{q-c}\|\cdot\left<(\mathbf{o-c})/\|\mathbf{o-c}\|,(\mathbf{q-c})/\|\mathbf{q-c}\|\right>+\left<\mathbf{o,c}\right>+\left<\mathbf{q,c}\right>-\|\mathbf{c}\|^{2}, where 𝐜\mathbf{c} is the centroid of the data vectors, and it reduces to the estimation of inner product between unit vectors as we do in Section 3.1.1., which further implies its potential in maximum inner product search and neural network quantization.

Appendix A The Proof of Lemma 3.1

Proof.

When 𝐨\mathbf{o} and 𝐪\mathbf{q} are collinear, i.e., 𝐪=−𝐨\mathbf{q}=-\mathbf{o} or 𝐪=𝐨\mathbf{q}=\mathbf{o}, (9) can be easily verified by definition. When 𝐨\mathbf{o} and 𝐪\mathbf{q} are non-collinear, they can be hosted in a two-dimensional subspace. We first find a pair of (mutually orthogonal unit) coordinate vectors of the subspace, i.e., 𝐨\mathbf{o} and 𝐞1:=𝐪−⟨𝐪,𝐨⟩​𝐨‖𝐪−⟨𝐪,𝐨⟩​𝐨‖\mathbf{e}_{1}:=\frac{\mathbf{q}-\left<\mathbf{q},\mathbf{o}\right>\mathbf{o}}{\|\mathbf{q}-\left<\mathbf{q},\mathbf{o}\right>\mathbf{o}\|}, which can be verified by

(23) ⟨𝐨,𝐞1⟩=\displaystyle\left<\mathbf{o},\mathbf{e}_{1}\right>= ⟨𝐨,𝐪−⟨𝐪,𝐨⟩​𝐨‖𝐪−⟨𝐪,𝐨⟩​𝐨‖⟩=⟨𝐪,𝐨⟩−⟨𝐪,𝐨⟩⋅‖𝐨‖2‖𝐪−⟨𝐪,𝐨⟩​𝐨‖=0\displaystyle\left<\mathbf{o},\frac{\mathbf{q}-\left<\mathbf{q},\mathbf{o}\right>\mathbf{o}}{\|\mathbf{q}-\left<\mathbf{q},\mathbf{o}\right>\mathbf{o}\|}\right>=\frac{\left<\mathbf{q,o}\right>-\left<\mathbf{q,o}\right>\cdot\|\mathbf{o}\|^{2}}{\|\mathbf{q}-\left<\mathbf{q},\mathbf{o}\right>\mathbf{o}\|}=0

We next decompose 𝐨¯\mathbf{\bar{o}} and 𝐪\mathbf{q} based on the coordinate vectors 𝐨\mathbf{o} and 𝐞1\mathbf{e}_{1} as follows.

(24) 𝐨¯=\displaystyle\mathbf{\bar{o}}= (𝐨¯−⟨𝐨¯,𝐨⟩​𝐨−⟨𝐨¯,𝐞1⟩​𝐞1)+⟨𝐨¯,𝐨⟩​𝐨+⟨𝐨¯,𝐞1⟩​𝐞1\displaystyle\left(\mathbf{\bar{o}}-\left<\mathbf{\bar{o}},\mathbf{o}\right>\mathbf{o}-\left<\mathbf{\bar{o}},\mathbf{e}_{1}\right>\mathbf{e}_{1}\right)+\left<\mathbf{\bar{o}},\mathbf{o}\right>\mathbf{o}+\left<\mathbf{\bar{o}},\mathbf{e}_{1}\right>\mathbf{e}_{1}
(25) 𝐪=\displaystyle\mathbf{q}= ⟨𝐪,𝐨⟩​𝐨+⟨𝐪,𝐞1⟩​𝐞1\displaystyle\left<\mathbf{q},\mathbf{o}\right>\mathbf{o}+\left<\mathbf{q},\mathbf{e}_{1}\right>\mathbf{e}_{1}

where (25) is because 𝐪\mathbf{q} is in the subspace. Then because (𝐨¯−⟨𝐨¯,𝐨⟩​𝐨−⟨𝐨¯,𝐞1⟩​𝐞1)\left(\mathbf{\bar{o}}-\left<\mathbf{\bar{o}},\mathbf{o}\right>\mathbf{o}-\left<\mathbf{\bar{o}},\mathbf{e}_{1}\right>\mathbf{e}_{1}\right) is orthogonal to the subspace and 𝐨⟂𝐞1\mathbf{o}\perp\mathbf{e}_{1}, we have

(26) ⟨𝐨¯,𝐪⟩=\displaystyle\left<\mathbf{\bar{o}},\mathbf{q}\right>= ⟨𝐨¯,𝐨⟩⋅⟨𝐨,𝐪⟩+⟨𝐨¯,𝐞1⟩⋅⟨𝐪,𝐞1⟩\displaystyle\left<\mathbf{\bar{o}},\mathbf{o}\right>\cdot\left<\mathbf{o},\mathbf{q}\right>+\left<\mathbf{\bar{o}},\mathbf{e}_{1}\right>\cdot\left<\mathbf{q},\mathbf{e}_{1}\right>
(27) =\displaystyle= ⟨𝐨¯,𝐨⟩⋅⟨𝐨,𝐪⟩+⟨𝐨¯,𝐞1⟩⋅1−⟨𝐨,𝐪⟩2\displaystyle\left<\mathbf{\bar{o}},\mathbf{o}\right>\cdot\left<\mathbf{o},\mathbf{q}\right>+\left<\mathbf{\bar{o}},\mathbf{e}_{1}\right>\cdot\sqrt{1-\left<\mathbf{o},\mathbf{q}\right>^{2}}

where (27) is due to the Pythagorean Theorem. ∎

Appendix B The Analysis for the Concentration Phenomenon

In this part, we provide rigorous analysis for the concentration phenomenon presented in Section 3.2.1. In particular, we will analyze the expected value of ⟨𝐨¯,𝐨⟩\left<\mathbf{\bar{o}},\mathbf{o}\right> (Section B.1), the extent of concentration of ⟨𝐨¯,𝐨⟩\left<\mathbf{\bar{o}},\mathbf{o}\right> (Section B.2) and the joint distribution of (⟨𝐨¯,𝐨⟩,⟨𝐨¯,𝐞1⟩)(\left<\mathbf{\bar{o}},\mathbf{o}\right>,\left<\mathbf{\bar{o}},\mathbf{e}_{1}\right>) (Section B.3). We summarize the conclusions in Lemma B.3 and empirically verify them in Figure 8.

B.1. The Expected Value of ⟨𝐨¯,𝐨⟩\left<\mathbf{\bar{o}},\mathbf{o}\right>

As is analyzed in Section 3.2.1, ⟨𝐨¯,𝐨⟩\left<\mathbf{\bar{o}},\mathbf{o}\right> and ⟨𝐨¯,𝐞1⟩\left<\mathbf{\bar{o}},\mathbf{e}_{1}\right> correspond to the projection of the random vector 𝐨¯\mathbf{\bar{o}} onto two mutually orthogonal directions. In order to analyze the joint distribution of the random variables, let us first revisit the process of the generation of 𝐨¯\mathbf{\bar{o}}. The generation of 𝐨¯\mathbf{\bar{o}} involves two steps. First, the algorithm randomly transforms a deterministic codebook 𝒞\mathcal{C} into 𝒞r​a​n​d\mathcal{C}_{rand} with a random orthogonal transformation PP. Second, it chooses the vector 𝐨¯\mathbf{\bar{o}} which has the largest inner product with 𝐨\mathbf{o} from the vectors in 𝒞r​a​n​d\mathcal{C}_{rand}. We next deduce from the definition (generation) of ⟨𝐨¯,𝐨⟩\left<\mathbf{\bar{o}},\mathbf{o}\right> as follows.

(28) ⟨𝐨¯,𝐨⟩=\displaystyle\left<\mathbf{\bar{o}},\mathbf{o}\right>= max𝐱∈C⁡⟨P​𝐱,𝐨⟩\displaystyle\max_{\mathbf{x}\in C}\left<P\mathbf{x},\mathbf{o}\right>
(29) =\displaystyle= max𝐱∈C⁡⟨𝐱,P−1​𝐨⟩=max⁡∑i=1D𝐱∈C⁡𝐱⁡[i]⋅(P−1​𝐨)​[i]\displaystyle\max_{\mathbf{x}\in C}\left<\mathbf{x},P^{-1}\mathbf{o}\right>=\max_{\mathbf{x}\in C}\sum_{i=1}^{D}\mathbf{x}[i]\cdot(P^{-1}\mathbf{o})[i]
(30) =\displaystyle= 1D​∑i=1D|(P−1​𝐨)​[i]|=1D​‖P−1​𝐨‖ℓ1\displaystyle\frac{1}{\sqrt{D}}\sum_{i=1}^{D}\left|(P^{-1}\mathbf{o})[i]\right|=\frac{1}{\sqrt{D}}\|P^{-1}\mathbf{o}\|_{\ell_{1}}

where (28) is due to the process of generation of 𝐨¯\mathbf{\bar{o}}. (29) is because the inner product is invariant to orthogonal transformation (rotation). (30) is due to the definition of our codebook 𝒞\mathcal{C} and the definition of ℓ1\ell_{1} norm. Specifically, as is analyzed in Section 3.1.3, the entry of 𝐱∈𝒞\mathbf{x}\in\mathcal{C} can only be 1/D1/\sqrt{D} or −1/D-1/\sqrt{D}. To maximize the inner product, we only need to pick the 𝐱\mathbf{x} which has its signs of the entries match the vector P−1​𝐨P^{-1}\mathbf{o}. Thus, the result of the inner product is the summation the absolute values as is presented in (30), where ∥⋅∥ℓ1\|\cdot\|_{\ell_{1}} is the ℓ1\ell_{1} norm.

We note that 𝐨\mathbf{o} is a unit vector. PP is a random orthogonal transformation matrix (i.e., random rotation), whose inverse matrix (inverse rotation) is also a random orthogonal transformation matrix. Thus, the vector P−1​𝐨P^{-1}\mathbf{o} follows the uniform distribution on the unit sphere 𝕊D−1\mathbb{S}^{D-1} in the DD-dimensional space ℝD\mathbb{R}^{D}. We note that the distribution is well studied (Khokhlov, 2006; Vershynin, 2018). We restate some conclusions about the distribution with the following lemma.

Lemma B.1.

((Khokhlov, 2006; Vershynin, 2018)) For a DD-dimensional random vector 𝐱=(𝐱⁡[1],𝐱⁡[2],…,𝐱⁡[D])\mathbf{x}=(\mathbf{x}[1],\mathbf{x}[2],...,\mathbf{x}[D]) which follows the uniform distribution on the unit sphere, the probability density function of its every coordinate 𝐱⁡[1],𝐱⁡[2],…,𝐱⁡[D]\mathbf{x}[1],\mathbf{x}[2],...,\mathbf{x}[D] is given as

(31) pD​(x)=Γ⁡(D2)π​Γ​(D−12)​(1−x2)D−32,x∈[−1,1]\displaystyle p_{D}(x)=\frac{\Gamma(\frac{D}{2})}{\sqrt{\pi}\Gamma(\frac{D-1}{2})}(1-x^{2})^{\frac{D-3}{2}},x\in[-1,1]

where Γ⁡(⋅)\Gamma(\cdot) is the Gamma function. The tail bound is given as

(32) ℙ{|𝐱[i]|>tD}≤2exp(−c0t2)\displaystyle\mathbb{P}\left\{\left|\mathbf{x}[i]\right|>\frac{t}{\sqrt{D}}\right\}\leq 2\exp\left(-c_{0}t^{2}\right)

where c0c_{0} is a constant, i=1,2,…,Di=1,2,...,D.

Based on the explicit expression of the probabilistic density function, we next derive the expected value of ⟨𝐨¯,𝐨⟩\left<\mathbf{\bar{o}},\mathbf{o}\right> as follows.

(33) 𝔼⁡[⟨𝐨¯,𝐨⟩]=\displaystyle\mathbb{E}\left[\left<\mathbf{\bar{o}},\mathbf{o}\right>\right]= 1D⋅𝔼⁡[∑i=1D|(P−1​𝐨)​[i]|]\displaystyle\frac{1}{\sqrt{D}}\cdot\mathbb{E}\left[\sum_{i=1}^{D}\left|(P^{-1}\mathbf{o})[i]\right|\right]
(34) =\displaystyle= D⋅𝔼⁡[|(P−1​𝐨)​[1]|]\displaystyle\sqrt{D}\cdot\mathbb{E}\left[\left|(P^{-1}\mathbf{o})[1]\right|\right]
(35) =\displaystyle= Dπ​Γ⁡(D2)Γ⁡(D−12)⋅∫−11(1−x2)D−32​|x|​𝑑x\displaystyle\sqrt{\frac{D}{\pi}}\frac{\Gamma(\frac{D}{2})}{\Gamma(\frac{D-1}{2})}\cdot\int_{-1}^{1}(1-x^{2})^{\frac{D-3}{2}}|x|\mathrm{d}x
(36) =\displaystyle= Dπ​2​Γ​(D2)(D−1)​Γ​(D−12)\displaystyle\sqrt{\frac{D}{\pi}}\frac{2\Gamma(\frac{D}{2})}{(D-1)\Gamma(\frac{D-1}{2})}

where (33) is due to (30). (34) is due to the linearity of expectation. (35) is due to Lemma B.1. (36) is by elementary calculus.

We note that although the expected value of ⟨𝐨¯,𝐨⟩\left<\mathbf{\bar{o}},\mathbf{o}\right> has a complicated form, i.e., (36), its numerical value is highly stable. When DD ranges from 10210^{2} to 10610^{6}, the value ranges from 0.798 to 0.800, which is verified by the observations in Section 3.2.1 perfectly.

B.2. The Concentration of ⟨𝐨¯,𝐨⟩\left<\mathbf{\bar{o}},\mathbf{o}\right>

We next analyze the extent of the concentration of ⟨𝐨¯,𝐨⟩\left<\mathbf{\bar{o}},\mathbf{o}\right>. Recall that as is shown in (30), ⟨𝐨¯,𝐨⟩=1D​‖P−1​𝐨‖ℓ1\left<\mathbf{\bar{o}},\mathbf{o}\right>=\frac{1}{\sqrt{D}}\|P^{-1}\mathbf{o}\|_{\ell_{1}}. Let f⁡(𝐱):=1D​‖𝐱‖ℓ1f(\mathbf{x}):=\frac{1}{\sqrt{D}}\|\mathbf{x}\|_{\ell_{1}}. Then ⟨𝐨¯,𝐨⟩=f⁡(P−1​𝐨)\left<\mathbf{\bar{o}},\mathbf{o}\right>=f(P^{-1}\mathbf{o}). We note that f⁡(𝐱)f(\mathbf{x}) is a Lipschitz function with the Lipschitz constant of 1, i.e.,

(37) |f⁡(𝐱)−f⁡(𝐲)|≤1⋅‖𝐱−𝐲‖\displaystyle\left|f(\mathbf{x})-f(\mathbf{y})\right|\leq 1\cdot\|\mathbf{x-y}\|

for every 𝐱,𝐲\mathbf{x,y} on the unit sphere.

Proof.
(38) |f⁡(𝐱)−f⁡(𝐲)|=1D​|‖𝐱‖ℓ1−‖𝐲‖ℓ1|\displaystyle\left|f(\mathbf{x})-f(\mathbf{y})\right|=\frac{1}{\sqrt{D}}\left|\|\mathbf{x}\|_{\ell_{1}}-\|\mathbf{y}\|_{\ell_{1}}\right|
(39) ≤\displaystyle\leq 1D​‖𝐱−𝐲‖ℓ1=1D​∑i=1D1⋅|𝐱⁡[i]−𝐲⁡[i]|\displaystyle\frac{1}{\sqrt{D}}\|\mathbf{x-y}\|_{\ell_{1}}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{D}}\sum_{i=1}^{D}1\cdot|\mathbf{x}[i]-\mathbf{y}[i]|
(40) ≤\displaystyle\leq 1D⋅∑i=1D12⋅∑i=1D(𝐱⁡[i]−𝐲⁡[i])2=‖𝐱−𝐲‖\displaystyle\frac{1}{\sqrt{D}}\cdot\sqrt{\sum_{i=1}^{D}1^{2}}\cdot\sqrt{\sum_{i=1}^{D}(\mathbf{x}[i]-\mathbf{y}[i])^{2}}=\|\mathbf{x-y}\|

where (38) is by definition. (39) is by triangle’s inequality. (40) is due to Cauchy-Schwarz inequality. ∎

Recall that P−1​𝐨P^{-1}\mathbf{o} is a random vector which follows the uniform distribution on the unit sphere. There is a well-known lemma (Vershynin, 2018) which presents that passing a random vector which follows the uniform distribution on the unit sphere through a Lipschitz function produces a highly concentrated distribution. The specific result is presented as follows.

Lemma B.2.

((Vershynin, 2018)) Let 𝐱\mathbf{x} be a DD-dimensional random vector which follows the uniform distribution on the unit sphere, f⁡(𝐱)f(\mathbf{x}) is a Lipschitz function with the Lipschitz constant of LL. Then

(41) ℙ{|f(𝐱)−𝔼[f(𝐱)]|≥t}≤2exp(−c​D​t2L2)\displaystyle\mathbb{P}\left\{\left|f(\mathbf{x})-\mathbb{E}\left[f(\mathbf{x})\right]\right|\geq t\right\}\leq 2\exp\left(-\frac{cDt^{2}}{L^{2}}\right)

where cc is a constant.

Plugging in our f⁡(𝐱)f(\mathbf{x}) immediately yields the following result.

(42) ℙ{|⟨𝐨¯,𝐨⟩−𝔼[⟨𝐨¯,𝐨⟩]|≥t}≤2exp(−cDt2)\displaystyle\mathbb{P}\left\{\left|\left<\mathbf{\bar{o}},\mathbf{o}\right>-\mathbb{E}\left[\left<\mathbf{\bar{o}},\mathbf{o}\right>\right]\right|\geq t\right\}\leq 2\exp\left(-cDt^{2}\right)
(43) ℙ{|⟨𝐨¯,𝐨⟩−𝔼[⟨𝐨¯,𝐨⟩]|≥uD}≤2exp(−cu2)\displaystyle\mathbb{P}\left\{\left|\left<\mathbf{\bar{o}},\mathbf{o}\right>-\mathbb{E}\left[\left<\mathbf{\bar{o}},\mathbf{o}\right>\right]\right|\geq\frac{u}{\sqrt{D}}\right\}\leq 2\exp\left(-cu^{2}\right)

where (43) is by letting u=t​Du=t\sqrt{D}. The conclusion shows that ⟨𝐨¯,𝐨⟩\left<\mathbf{\bar{o}},\mathbf{o}\right> is highly concentrated around its expectation. It will not deviate from its expectation by Ω⁡(1/D)\Omega(1/\sqrt{D}) with high probability.

B.3. The Joint Distribution of (⟨𝐨¯,𝐨⟩,⟨𝐨¯,𝐞1⟩)(\left<\mathbf{\bar{o}},\mathbf{o}\right>,\left<\mathbf{\bar{o}},\mathbf{e}_{1}\right>)

We next analyze the distribution of ⟨𝐨¯,𝐞1⟩\left<\mathbf{\bar{o}},\mathbf{e}_{1}\right>. Recall that the randomness of both ⟨𝐨¯,𝐨⟩\left<\mathbf{\bar{o}},\mathbf{o}\right> and ⟨𝐨¯,𝐞1⟩\left<\mathbf{\bar{o}},\mathbf{e}_{1}\right> is due to the randomness of 𝐨¯\mathbf{\bar{o}} (which is further due to the randomness of PP). These random variables are correlated with each other, which is undesirable for subsequent analysis. We first consider decorrelating the random variables by representing ⟨𝐨¯,𝐞1⟩\left<\mathbf{\bar{o}},\mathbf{e}_{1}\right> with a function of ⟨𝐨¯,𝐨⟩\left<\mathbf{\bar{o}},\mathbf{o}\right> and a random variable which is independent to ⟨𝐨¯,𝐨⟩\left<\mathbf{\bar{o}},\mathbf{o}\right>. In particular, we will show that the joint distribution of (⟨𝐨¯,𝐨⟩,⟨𝐨¯,𝐞1⟩)(\left<\mathbf{\bar{o}},\mathbf{o}\right>,\left<\mathbf{\bar{o}},\mathbf{e}_{1}\right>) is identical to that of

(44) (⟨𝐨¯,𝐨⟩,1−⟨𝐨¯,𝐨⟩2⋅X1)\displaystyle\left(\left<\mathbf{\bar{o}},\mathbf{o}\right>,\sqrt{1-\left<\mathbf{\bar{o}},\mathbf{o}\right>^{2}}\cdot X_{1}\right)

where X1X_{1} follows the distribution of pD−1p_{D-1} in Lemma B.1 and is independent to ⟨𝐨¯,𝐨⟩\left<\mathbf{\bar{o}},\mathbf{o}\right>.

Proof.

Let 𝐮1=(1,0,0,…,0),𝐮2=(0,1,0,…,0)\mathbf{u}_{1}=(1,0,0,...,0),\mathbf{u}_{2}=(0,1,0,...,0). For 𝐨\mathbf{o} and 𝐞1\mathbf{e}_{1} where 𝐨⟂𝐞1\mathbf{o}\perp\mathbf{e}_{1}, there exists an orthogonal matrix UU to align them on 𝐮1\mathbf{u}_{1} and 𝐮2\mathbf{u}_{2}, i.e., U​𝐨=𝐮1,U​𝐞1=𝐮2U\mathbf{o}=\mathbf{u}_{1},U\mathbf{e}_{1}=\mathbf{u}_{2}. Then by applying the orthogonal matrix UU to both sides of the inner products, we have 𝐱¯=arg​max𝐱∈𝒞⁡⟨UP​𝐱,𝐮1⟩\mathbf{\bar{x}}=\argmax_{\mathbf{x}\in\mathcal{C}}\left<UP\mathbf{x},\mathbf{u}_{1}\right>, ⟨P​𝐱¯,𝐨⟩=⟨U​P​𝐱¯,𝐮1⟩\left<P\mathbf{\bar{x}},\mathbf{o}\right>=\left<UP\mathbf{\bar{x}},\mathbf{u}_{1}\right> and ⟨P​𝐱¯,𝐞1⟩=⟨U​P​𝐱¯,𝐮2⟩\left<P\mathbf{\bar{x}},\mathbf{e}_{1}\right>=\left<UP\mathbf{\bar{x}},\mathbf{u}_{2}\right>. Thus, to prove the original statement, it is equivalent to prove that the joint distribution of (⟨U​P​𝐱¯,𝐮1⟩,⟨U​P​𝐱¯,𝐮2⟩)(\left<UP\mathbf{\bar{x}},\mathbf{u}_{1}\right>,\left<UP\mathbf{\bar{x}},\mathbf{u}_{2}\right>) is identical to that of

(45) (⟨U​P​𝐱¯,𝐮1⟩,1−⟨U​P​𝐱¯,𝐮1⟩2⋅X1)\displaystyle\left(\left<UP\mathbf{\bar{x}},\mathbf{u}_{1}\right>,\sqrt{1-\left<UP\mathbf{\bar{x}},\mathbf{u}_{1}\right>^{2}}\cdot X_{1}\right)

where X1X_{1} is independent to ⟨U​P​𝐱¯,𝐮1⟩\left<UP\mathbf{\bar{x}},\mathbf{u}_{1}\right> and X1∼pD−1X_{1}\sim p_{D-1}. Because the random orthogonal transformation is rotation-invariant, i.e., the distribution of U​PUP is identical to the distribution of PP, we can substitute all the U​PUP with PP. Then the statement reduces to the same form as the original one while replacing 𝐨\mathbf{o} and 𝐞1\mathbf{e}_{1} with 𝐮1\mathbf{u}_{1} and 𝐮2\mathbf{u}_{2}, respectively. Thus, in order to prove the statement for a general pair of 𝐨\mathbf{o} and 𝐞1\mathbf{e}_{1}, it suffices to prove the case of 𝐨=𝐮1\mathbf{o}=\mathbf{u}_{1} and 𝐞1=𝐮2\mathbf{e}_{1}=\mathbf{u}_{2} without loss of generality. We next prove the case of 𝐮1,𝐮2\mathbf{u}_{1},\mathbf{u}_{2}.

We consider analyzing the distribution based on the Principle of Deferred Decision (Motwani and Raghavan, 1995). The basic idea of the Principle of Deferred Decision is that for a randomized algorithm which needs sample several random numbers, we assume that the sampling operation happens at the time when the algorithm accesses the sampled numbers instead of happening in the very beginning. In our case, recall that we will sample a random orthogonal matrix PP. Its generation involves sampling D×DD\times D of standard Gaussian random variables as its entries and orthonormalizing the matrix with the Gram–Schmidt orthonormalization. We note that the Gram–Schmidt orthonormalization proceeds row by row. In particular, assuming that the first i−1i-1 rows of PP, i.e., 𝐩1,…,𝐩i−1\mathbf{p}_{1},...,\mathbf{p}_{i-1}, have been orthonormalized (i.e., 𝐩j⟂𝐩k,‖𝐩j‖=‖𝐩k‖=1,∀1≤j<k≤i−1\mathbf{p}_{j}\perp\mathbf{p}_{k},\|\mathbf{p}_{j}\|=\|\mathbf{p}_{k}\|=1,\forall 1\leq j<k\leq i-1), we orthonormalize the first ii row by letting 𝐩i\mathbf{p}_{i} be

(46) 𝐩i=𝐠−∑j=1i−1⟨𝐠,𝐩j⟩​𝐩j‖𝐠−∑j=1i−1⟨𝐠,𝐩j⟩​𝐩j‖\displaystyle\mathbf{p}_{i}=\frac{\mathbf{g}-\sum_{j=1}^{i-1}\left<\mathbf{g},\mathbf{p}_{j}\right>\mathbf{p}_{j}}{\left\|\mathbf{g}-\sum_{j=1}^{i-1}\left<\mathbf{g},\mathbf{p}_{j}\right>\mathbf{p}_{j}\right\|}

where the entries of 𝐠\mathbf{g} are sampled from a standard random Gaussian distribution. Thus, due to the process of Gram–Schmidt orthonormalization, the sampling process can be viewed as a sequential process of DD steps where in each step we sample a new row.

In our algorithm, we note that the joint distribution of (⟨P​𝐱¯,𝐮1⟩,⟨P​𝐱¯,𝐮2⟩)(\left<P\mathbf{\bar{x}},\mathbf{u}_{1}\right>,\left<P\mathbf{\bar{x}},\mathbf{u}_{2}\right>) depends only on the first two row of PP. Let us first sample the first row of PP, i.e., 𝐩1\mathbf{p}_{1}. Then 𝐱¯\mathbf{\bar{x}} is determined because

(47) 𝐱¯\displaystyle\mathbf{\bar{x}} =arg​max𝐱∈𝒞⁡⟨P​𝐱,𝐮1⟩=arg​max𝐱∈𝒞⁡⟨𝐱,P−1​𝐮1⟩\displaystyle=\argmax_{\mathbf{x\in\mathcal{C}}}\left<P\mathbf{x},\mathbf{u}_{1}\right>=\argmax_{\mathbf{x\in\mathcal{C}}}\left<\mathbf{x},P^{-1}\mathbf{u}_{1}\right>
(48) =arg​max𝐱∈𝒞⁡⟨𝐱,P⊤​𝐮1⟩=arg​max𝐱∈𝒞⁡⟨𝐱,𝐩1⟩\displaystyle=\argmax_{\mathbf{x\in\mathcal{C}}}\left<\mathbf{x},P^{\top}\mathbf{u}_{1}\right>=\argmax_{\mathbf{x\in\mathcal{C}}}\left<\mathbf{x},\mathbf{p}_{1}\right>

where (48) is because the inverse of an orthogonal matrix equals to its transpose. For the fixed 𝐱¯\mathbf{\bar{x}}, we next analyze the distribution of ⟨P​𝐱¯,𝐮2⟩\left<P\mathbf{\bar{x}},\mathbf{u}_{2}\right>. We note that similarlly, it depends only on the first two rows of PP because ⟨P​𝐱¯,𝐮2⟩=⟨𝐱¯,𝐩2⟩\left<P\mathbf{\bar{x}},\mathbf{u}_{2}\right>=\left<\mathbf{\bar{x}},\mathbf{p}_{2}\right> (recall that 𝐱¯\mathbf{\bar{x}} depends on 𝐩1\mathbf{p}_{1}). For the vector 𝐩1\mathbf{p}_{1} and 𝐱¯\mathbf{\bar{x}}, there exists an orthogonal matrix VV to align them on 𝐯1=(1,0,0,…,0)\mathbf{v}_{1}=(1,0,0,...,0) and 𝐯2=(⟨𝐱¯,𝐩1⟩,1−⟨𝐱¯,𝐩1⟩2,0,…,0)\mathbf{v}_{2}=(\left<\mathbf{\bar{x}},\mathbf{p}_{1}\right>,\sqrt{1-\left<\mathbf{\bar{x}},\mathbf{p}_{1}\right>^{2}},0,...,0), i.e., 𝐯1=V​𝐩1\mathbf{v}_{1}=V\mathbf{p}_{1} and 𝐯2=V​𝐱¯\mathbf{v}_{2}=V\mathbf{\bar{x}}. Then

(49) ⟨𝐱¯,𝐩2⟩\displaystyle\left<\mathbf{\bar{x}},\mathbf{p}_{2}\right> =⟨𝐱¯,𝐠−⟨𝐠,𝐩𝟏⟩​𝐩𝟏‖𝐠−⟨𝐠,𝐩𝟏⟩​𝐩𝟏‖⟩\displaystyle=\left<\mathbf{\bar{x}},\frac{\mathbf{g}-\left<\mathbf{g},\mathbf{p_{1}}\right>\mathbf{p_{1}}}{\|\mathbf{g}-\left<\mathbf{g},\mathbf{p_{1}}\right>\mathbf{p_{1}}\|}\right>
(50) =⟨V​𝐱¯,V​𝐠−⟨V​𝐠,V​𝐩𝟏⟩​V​𝐩𝟏‖V​𝐠−⟨V​𝐠,V​𝐩𝟏⟩​V​𝐩𝟏‖⟩\displaystyle=\left<V\mathbf{\bar{x}},\frac{V\mathbf{g}-\left<V\mathbf{g},V\mathbf{p_{1}}\right>V\mathbf{p_{1}}}{\|V\mathbf{g}-\left<V\mathbf{g},V\mathbf{p_{1}}\right>V\mathbf{p_{1}}\|}\right>
(51) =⟨𝐯2,𝐠−⟨𝐠,𝐯𝟏⟩​𝐯𝟏‖𝐠−⟨𝐠,𝐯𝟏⟩​𝐯𝟏‖⟩\displaystyle=\left<\mathbf{v}_{2},\frac{\mathbf{g}-\left<\mathbf{g},\mathbf{v_{1}}\right>\mathbf{v_{1}}}{\|\mathbf{g}-\left<\mathbf{g},\mathbf{v_{1}}\right>\mathbf{v_{1}}\|}\right>

where (49) is by Gram-Schmidt orthonormalization. (50) is because inner product and Euclidean distance are invariant to orthogonal transformation. (51) is because standard Gaussian random vector is rotational-invariant (Vershynin, 2018), i.e., V​𝐠V\mathbf{g} and 𝐠\mathbf{g} are identically distributed. We note that 𝐯1\mathbf{v}_{1} only has its first entry non-zero. Thus, 𝐠−⟨𝐠,𝐯𝟏⟩​𝐯𝟏\mathbf{g}-\left<\mathbf{g},\mathbf{v_{1}}\right>\mathbf{v_{1}} has the first dimension of 0 and has its remaining D−1D-1 dimensions to be independent standard Gaussian variables. After normalization, the remaining D−1D-1 dimensions follow the uniform distribution on unit sphere in the (D−1)(D-1)-dimensional space and are independent to 𝐩1\mathbf{p}_{1}. Recall that 𝐯2=(⟨𝐩1,𝐱¯⟩,1−⟨𝐩1,𝐱¯⟩2,0,…,0)\mathbf{v}_{2}=(\left<\mathbf{p}_{1},\mathbf{\bar{x}}\right>,\sqrt{1-\left<\mathbf{p}_{1},\mathbf{\bar{x}}\right>^{2}},0,...,0). Thus, ⟨𝐱¯,𝐩2⟩=1−⟨𝐩1,𝐱¯⟩2⋅X1\left<\mathbf{\bar{x}},\mathbf{p}_{2}\right>=\sqrt{1-\left<\mathbf{p}_{1},\mathbf{\bar{x}}\right>^{2}}\cdot X_{1} where X1X_{1} follows the distribution of pD−1p_{D-1}. ∎

We summarize our conclusions about the distribution of (⟨𝐨¯,𝐨⟩,⟨𝐨¯,𝐞1⟩)(\left<\mathbf{\bar{o}},\mathbf{o}\right>,\left<\mathbf{\bar{o}},\mathbf{e}_{1}\right>) with the following lemma.

Lemma B.3 (Distribution).

Let 𝐨\mathbf{o} and 𝐞1\mathbf{e}_{1} be two unit vectors, where 𝐨⟂𝐞1\mathbf{o}\perp\mathbf{e}_{1}. Let PP be a random orthogonal transformation matrix, 𝒞\mathcal{C} be our constructed deterministic codebook and 𝐱¯=arg​max𝐱∈𝒞⁡⟨P​𝐱,𝐨⟩\mathbf{\bar{x}}=\argmax_{\mathbf{x}\in\mathcal{C}}\left<P\mathbf{x},\mathbf{o}\right>, 𝐨¯=P​𝐱¯\mathbf{\bar{o}}=P\mathbf{\bar{x}}. Then the joint distribution of (⟨𝐨¯,𝐨⟩,⟨𝐨¯,𝐞1⟩)(\left<\mathbf{\bar{o}},\mathbf{o}\right>,\left<\mathbf{\bar{o}},\mathbf{e}_{1}\right>) is identical to that of

(52) (⟨𝐨¯,𝐨⟩,1−⟨𝐨¯,𝐨⟩2⋅X1)\displaystyle\left(\left<\mathbf{\bar{o}},\mathbf{o}\right>,\sqrt{1-\left<\mathbf{\bar{o}},\mathbf{o}\right>^{2}}\cdot X_{1}\right)

where X1X_{1} is independent to ⟨𝐨¯,𝐨⟩\left<\mathbf{\bar{o}},\mathbf{o}\right> and X1∼pD−1X_{1}\sim p_{D-1}. The expected value of ⟨𝐨¯,𝐨⟩\left<\mathbf{\bar{o}},\mathbf{o}\right> is

(53) 𝔼⁡[⟨𝐨¯,𝐨⟩]=Dπ⋅2​Γ​(D2)(D−1)​Γ​(D−12)\displaystyle\mathbb{E}\left[\left<\mathbf{\bar{o}},\mathbf{o}\right>\right]=\sqrt{\frac{D}{\pi}}\cdot\frac{2\Gamma(\frac{D}{2})}{(D-1)\Gamma(\frac{D-1}{2})}

where Γ⁡(⋅)\Gamma(\cdot) is the Gamma function. Its concentration bound is

(54) ℙ{|⟨𝐨¯,𝐨⟩−𝔼[⟨𝐨¯,𝐨⟩]|>uD}≤2exp(−cu2)\displaystyle\mathbb{P}\left\{\left|\left<\mathbf{\bar{o}},\mathbf{o}\right>-\mathbb{E}\left[\left<\mathbf{\bar{o}},\mathbf{o}\right>\right]\right|>\frac{u}{\sqrt{D}}\right\}\leq 2\exp\left(-cu^{2}\right)

where cc in a constant.

We next provide empirical verification for the theorem in Figure 8. First, in the upper panel of Figure 8, the orange histogram represents the empirical distribution of ⟨𝐨¯,𝐞1⟩1−⟨𝐨¯,𝐨⟩2\frac{\left<\mathbf{\bar{o}},\mathbf{e}_{1}\right>}{\sqrt{1-\left<\mathbf{\bar{o}},\mathbf{o}\right>^{2}}} based on the 10510^{5} samples of PP in Section 3.2.1. Due to (52), it follows the distribution of pD−1p_{D-1}. The red curve plots the theoretical density function of pD−1p_{D-1} as is specified in Lemma B.1. It shows that the empirical results and the theoretical results match perfectly, which verifies the correctness of our analysis. Second, in the lower panel of Figure 8, the orange histogram represents the empirical distribution of ⟨P​𝐱¯,𝐨⟩\left<P\mathbf{\bar{x}},\mathbf{o}\right> based on the aforementioned 10510^{5} samples. It shows that ⟨P​𝐱¯,𝐨⟩\left<P\mathbf{\bar{x}},\mathbf{o}\right> is indeed highly concentrated around its mean value and the empirical mean value matches the theoretical expectation perfectly, which verifies our theoretical analysis.

Appendix D The Analysis for BqB_{q}

In this section, we prove that Bq=Θ⁡(log⁡log⁡D)B_{q}=\Theta(\log\log D) suffices to guarantee that the error introduced by the uniform scalar quantization is much smaller than the error of the estimator itself, i.e., O⁡(1/D)O(1/\sqrt{D}). We prove the statement in two steps. First, we will prove that the error introduced by the uniform scalar quantization is O⁡(Δ)O(\Delta) in Section D.1 (recall that Δ=(max⁡𝐪′​[i]−min⁡𝐪′​[i])/(2Bq−1)\Delta=\left(\max\mathbf{q^{\prime}}[i]-\min\mathbf{q^{\prime}}[i]\right)/(2^{B_{q}}-1)). Specifically, recall that we approximately compute ⟨𝐱¯,𝐪′⟩\left<\mathbf{\bar{x}},\mathbf{q}^{\prime}\right> as ⟨𝐱¯,𝐪¯⟩\left<\mathbf{\bar{x}},\mathbf{\bar{q}}\right>. Then the error equals to |⟨𝐱¯,𝐪¯−𝐪′⟩|\left|\left<\mathbf{\bar{x}},\mathbf{\bar{q}}-\mathbf{q}^{\prime}\right>\right|. Note that 𝐱¯\mathbf{\bar{x}} has its entries of ±1/D\pm 1/\sqrt{D} and 𝐪¯​[i]−𝐪′​[i]∈[−Δ,Δ]\mathbf{\bar{q}}[i]-\mathbf{q}^{\prime}[i]\in[-\Delta,\Delta]. Then a trivial bound by the triangle’s inequality yields |⟨𝐱¯,𝐪¯−𝐪′⟩|≤D⋅1D⋅Δ=D⋅Δ\left|\left<\mathbf{\bar{x}},\mathbf{\bar{q}}-\mathbf{q}^{\prime}\right>\right|\leq D\cdot\frac{1}{\sqrt{D}}\cdot\Delta=\sqrt{D}\cdot\Delta. We note that the bound is weak because it does not consider the cancellation of under-estimate and over-estimate. We will prove a stronger probabilistic bound of O⁡(Δ)O(\Delta) by considering the randomized uniform scalar quantization algorithm presented in Section 3.3.1 and quantitatively analyzing the cancellation. Second, we will prove that Δ=O⁡(log⁡DD/2Bq)\Delta=O(\sqrt{\frac{\log D}{D}}/2^{B_{q}}) in Section D.2. Recall that 𝐪′=P−1​𝐪\mathbf{q}^{\prime}=P^{-1}\mathbf{q} is a random vector which follows the uniform distribution on the unit sphere. A trivial bound gives that (max⁡𝐪′​[i]−min⁡𝐪′​[i])=O⁡(1)\left(\max\mathbf{q^{\prime}}[i]-\min\mathbf{q^{\prime}}[i]\right)=O(1). We note that the bound is weak because it does not consider the concentration phenomenon of the entries of 𝐪′\mathbf{q^{\prime}} (see Lemma B.1). We will prove a stronger probabilistic bound by quantitatively considering the concentration phenomenon.

Based on the two probabilistic bounds, we derive the overall error by applying the union bound. The conclusions are summarized in Table 5. Making the overall error be O⁡(1/D)O(1/\sqrt{D}), we have Bq=Θ⁡(log⁡log⁡D)B_{q}=\Theta(\log\log D). We note that based on the trivial bounds, it is necessary to set Bq=Θ⁡(log⁡D)B_{q}=\Theta(\log D) to guarantee the same error bound, which is exponentially worse than our result.

D.1. The Error of Randomized Uniform Scalar Quantization

As is discussed above, the error introduced by the uniform scalar quantization is

(63) |⟨𝐱¯,𝐪¯−𝐪′⟩|=|∑i=1D𝐱¯​[i]⋅(𝐪¯​[i]−𝐪′​[i])|\displaystyle\left|\left<\mathbf{\bar{x}},\mathbf{\bar{q}}-\mathbf{q}^{\prime}\right>\right|=\left|\sum_{i=1}^{D}\mathbf{\bar{x}}[i]\cdot(\mathbf{\bar{q}}[i]-\mathbf{q}^{\prime}[i])\right|

Due to the randomized uniform scalar quantization presented in Section 3.3.1, each term of the error, i.e., 𝐱¯​[i]⋅(𝐪¯​[i]−𝐪′​[i])\mathbf{\bar{x}}[i]\cdot(\mathbf{\bar{q}}[i]-\mathbf{q}^{\prime}[i]), is a random variable. The DD random variables are independent to each other. Each term has the expected value of 0 (see Section 3.3.1) and has their values bounded by [−Δ/D,+Δ/D][-\Delta/\sqrt{D},+\Delta/\sqrt{D}]. Now the question is to analyze the summation of DD such random variables. We note that the Hoeffding’s inequality immediately answers the question (Vershynin, 2018). We restate the inequality in the following lemma.

Lemma D.1 (Hoeffding’s Inequality (Vershynin, 2018)).

Let X1,…,XnX_{1},...,X_{n} be independent random variables, such that Xi∈[ai,bi],∀1≤i≤nX_{i}\in[a_{i},b_{i}],\forall 1\leq i\leq n. Let Sn=∑i=1nXiS_{n}=\sum_{i=1}^{n}X_{i}. Then

(64) ℙ{|Sn−𝔼[Sn]|≥t}≤2exp(−2​t2∑i=1n(bi−ai)2)\displaystyle\mathbb{P}\left\{\left|S_{n}-\mathbb{E}\left[S_{n}\right]\right|\geq t\right\}\leq 2\exp\left(-\frac{2t^{2}}{\sum_{i=1}^{n}(b_{i}-a_{i})^{2}}\right)

In our case, we note that ai=−Δ/Da_{i}=-\Delta/\sqrt{D}, bi=+Δ/Db_{i}=+\Delta/\sqrt{D}. 𝔼⁡[Sn]=𝔼⁡[∑i=1nXi]=∑i=1n𝔼⁡[Xi]=0\mathbb{E}\left[S_{n}\right]=\mathbb{E}\left[\sum_{i=1}^{n}X_{i}\right]=\sum_{i=1}^{n}\mathbb{E}\left[X_{i}\right]=0. It immediately yields the following conclusion.

(65) ℙ{|∑i=1D𝐱¯[i]⋅(𝐪¯[i]−𝐪′[i])|≥t}≤2exp(−t22​Δ2)\displaystyle\mathbb{P}\left\{\left|\sum_{i=1}^{D}\mathbf{\bar{x}}[i]\cdot(\mathbf{\bar{q}}[i]-\mathbf{q}^{\prime}[i])\right|\geq t\right\}\leq 2\exp\left(-\frac{t^{2}}{2\Delta^{2}}\right)
(66) ℙ{|∑i=1D𝐱¯[i]⋅(𝐪¯[i]−𝐪′[i])|≥Δu}≤2exp(−u22)\displaystyle\mathbb{P}\left\{\left|\sum_{i=1}^{D}\mathbf{\bar{x}}[i]\cdot(\mathbf{\bar{q}}[i]-\mathbf{q}^{\prime}[i])\right|\geq\Delta u\right\}\leq 2\exp\left(-\frac{u^{2}}{2}\right)

where (66) is by letting u=t/Δu=t/\Delta. The conclusion shows that the error is bounded by O⁡(Δ)O(\Delta) with high probability.

Appendix E Discussion on the Normalization

We note that our current theoretical analysis (without any assumptions on the data) provides an additive error bound like (Alon and Klartag, 2017). Let d​i​s​t′2dist^{\prime 2} be the estimated squared distance based on our estimator, where d​i​s​t′2=‖𝐨r−𝐜‖2+‖𝐪r−𝐜‖2−2⋅‖𝐨r−𝐜‖⋅‖𝐪r−𝐜‖⋅⟨𝐨¯,𝐪⟩⟨𝐨¯,𝐨⟩dist^{\prime 2}=\|\mathbf{o}_{r}-\mathbf{c}\|^{2}+\|\mathbf{q}_{r}-\mathbf{c}\|^{2}-2\cdot\|\mathbf{o}_{r}-\mathbf{c}\|\cdot\|\mathbf{q}_{r}-\mathbf{c}\|\cdot\frac{\left<\mathbf{\bar{o}},\mathbf{q}\right>}{\left<\mathbf{\bar{o}},\mathbf{o}\right>}. Considering that we do not normalize the dataset with the centroids but with the origin of the space, then based on the Equation (15) in Theorem 3.2, we immediately have

(71) |d​i​s​t′2−‖𝐨r−𝐪r‖2|=‖𝐨r‖⋅‖𝐪r‖⋅O⁡(1D)​w.h.p.\displaystyle\left|dist^{\prime 2}-\|\mathbf{o}_{r}-\mathbf{q}_{r}\|^{2}\right|=\|\mathbf{o}_{r}\|\cdot\|\mathbf{q}_{r}\|\cdot O\left(\frac{1}{\sqrt{D}}\right)\ w.h.p.

where w.h.p. is short for “with high probability”.

When the data vectors are well normalized and spread evenly on the unit hypersphere, we assume that the data vector after normalization, i.e., 𝐨=𝐨r−𝐜‖𝐨r−𝐜‖\mathbf{o}=\frac{\mathbf{o}_{r}-\mathbf{c}}{\|\mathbf{o}_{r}-\mathbf{c}\|}, follows the uniform distribution on the unit hypersphere. Then we can derive the following corollary which presents a multiplicative error bound like (Indyk and Wagner, 2022).

Corollary E.1.

Assuming that 𝐨\mathbf{o} follows the uniform distribution on the unit hypersphere. We have

(72) |d​i​s​t′2−‖𝐨r−𝐪r‖2‖𝐨r−𝐪r‖2|=O⁡(1D)​w.h.p.\displaystyle\left|\frac{dist^{\prime 2}-\|\mathbf{o}_{r}-\mathbf{q}_{r}\|^{2}}{\|\mathbf{o}_{r}-\mathbf{q}_{r}\|^{2}}\right|=O\left(\frac{1}{\sqrt{D}}\right)\ w.h.p.
Proof.
(73) |d​i​s​t′2−‖𝐪r−𝐨r‖2‖𝐪r−𝐨r‖2|=|2​‖𝐪r−𝐜‖​‖𝐨r−𝐜‖‖𝐪r−𝐨r‖2|⋅O⁡(1D)\displaystyle\left|\frac{dist^{\prime 2}-\|\mathbf{q}_{r}-\mathbf{o}_{r}\|^{2}}{\|\mathbf{q}_{r}-\mathbf{o}_{r}\|^{2}}\right|=\left|\frac{2\|\mathbf{q}_{r}-\mathbf{c}\|\|\mathbf{o}_{r}-\mathbf{c}\|}{\|\mathbf{q}_{r}-\mathbf{o}_{r}\|^{2}}\right|\cdot O\left(\frac{1}{\sqrt{D}}\right)
(74) =\displaystyle= |2​‖𝐪r−𝐜‖​‖𝐨r−𝐜‖‖𝐪r−𝐜‖2+‖𝐨r−𝐜‖2−2​⟨𝐨r−𝐜,𝐪r−𝐜⟩|⋅O⁡(1D)\displaystyle\left|\frac{2\|\mathbf{q}_{r}-\mathbf{c}\|\|\mathbf{o}_{r}-\mathbf{c}\|}{\|\mathbf{q}_{r}-\mathbf{c}\|^{2}+\|\mathbf{o}_{r}-\mathbf{c}\|^{2}-2\left<\mathbf{o}_{r}-\mathbf{c},\mathbf{q}_{r}-\mathbf{c}\right>}\right|\cdot O\left(\frac{1}{\sqrt{D}}\right)
(75) =\displaystyle= |112​(‖𝐪r−𝐜‖‖𝐨r−𝐜‖+‖𝐨r−𝐜‖‖𝐪r−𝐜‖)−⟨𝐨,𝐪⟩|⋅O⁡(1D)\displaystyle\left|\frac{1}{\frac{1}{2}\left(\frac{\|\mathbf{q}_{r}-\mathbf{c}\|}{\|\mathbf{o}_{r}-\mathbf{c}\|}+\frac{\|\mathbf{o}_{r}-\mathbf{c}\|}{\|\mathbf{q}_{r}-\mathbf{c}\|}\right)-\left<\mathbf{o},\mathbf{q}\right>}\right|\cdot O\left(\frac{1}{\sqrt{D}}\right)

where (73) is due to (71). (74) is by elementary linear algebra. (75) simplifies (74). The first inequality of (76) is due to the numerical inequality that (x+1x)≥2,∀x>0\left(x+\frac{1}{x}\right)\geq 2,\forall x>0. The second equality of (76) holds because 𝐨\mathbf{o} follows the uniform distribution on the unit hypersphere. In particular, due to the concentration inequality (Lemma B.1), ⟨𝐨,𝐪⟩\left<\mathbf{o},\mathbf{q}\right> is highly concentrated around 0, e.g., it has sufficiently high probability to be upper bounded by 12\frac{1}{2}. ∎

We emphasize that the corollary is not fully rigorous as it depends on the assumption that 𝐨\mathbf{o} follows the uniform distribution on the unit hypersphere. Note that all our other theoretical results do not rely on any assumptions on the data, i.e., the additive bound holds regardless of the data distribution. In the present work, we only adopt a simple and natural method of normalization (i.e., with the centroids of IVF) to instantiate our scheme of quantization, while we have yet to extensively explore the normalization step itself. We shall leave it as future work to thoroughly and rigorously study the normalization problem.

To verify the effectiveness of the current method of normalization, we measure the empirical uniformity of the normalized data vectors with the entropy of each bit in our quantization codes 99 9 In our quantization codes, let pp be the proportion of 1’s in the iith bit of the whole dataset. Then the entropy of the iith bit equals to −[p​log2⁡(p)+(1−p)​log2⁡(1−p)]-[p\log_{2}(p)+(1-p)\log_{2}(1-p)]. We report the summation of the entropy over all the bits. The result is normalized by the length of the quantization codes for the ease of study.. The larger the entropy is, the more uniform the normalized dataset is (and at the same time, the more informative the quantization codes are). We report that on all the datasets, the entropy is over 99.9% of the length of the quantization codes (in other word, for every bit in the quantization codes, the number of 1’s is almost the same as the number of 0’s), indicating that normalizing the dataset with the centroids of IVF is empirically effective.

Appendix F Discussion on the Ablation Study

We emphasize that RaBitQ is a method with rigorous theoretical guarantee. The newly proposed codebook construction and distance estimation are an integral whole. The ablation of any component will cause the loss of the theoretical guarantee (i.e., the performance is no more theoretically predictable) and further disable the error-bound-based re-ranking for ANN (Section 4). We summarize the dependency of the theoretical conclusions and efficient implementations on our algorithm components in detail in Figure 9. The green, blue and orange boxes represent the components in our algorithm, the theoretical conclusions and the implementations respectively. An arrow indicates that a particular component or theoretical conclusion is used for achieving the downstream conclusion or implementation. In addition, we would also like to highlight that although RaBitQ achieves the asymptotic optimality in terms of the worst-case error bound, for datasets which have certain promising properties, it is still possible to obtain better empirical performance via further (possibly heuristic) optimization. We believe this is an interesting research topic and we would like to leave it as future work.

Despite that the ablation is irrational in view of theory, we provide several empirical studies to discuss how each component empirically affects the performance 1010 10 Recall that the error-bound-based re-ranking would be disabled when any of the components is ablated. Using it for ANN entails exhaustive tuning of the parameters of re-ranking, which would heavily affect the results of ANN search. Thus, the results of ANN would be less insightful for an ablation study. We only report the results of distance estimation.. We investigate the effects of removing a certain component from RaBitQ while keeping the others.

F.1. The Ablation of the Codebook Construction

Recall that in Section 3.1, for quantizing a set of normalized data vectors, we construct a quantization codebook by randomly rotating a set of bi-valued vectors. We consider replacing our randomized codebook with a learned heuristic codebook of PQ while keeping other components. We note that with our randomized codebook, RaBitQ has rigorous theoretical guarantee and achieves asymptotic optimality. However, with a learned heuristic codebook, the performance of the method will be no more theoretically predictable. Though it is often intuitive to expect that replacing a randomized algorithm with a learned algorithm may improve the performance, in RaBitQ, whose design is an integral whole, a learned codebook could be less suitable than a randomized codebook. Table 6 presents the average relative error and maximum relative error of the ablation study on the GIST dataset. It clearly shows that replacing a randomized codebook with a learned one degrades both the general quality and the robustness of distance estimation. The results imply that despite that PQ, as a learning-based method, has a large search space of codebooks, the heuristic learning process (which is based on a heuristic objective function and an approximate optimization algorithm) only finds a suboptimal solution among the search space. Similar findings can be observed in the main experiments (Section 5.2.1), i.e., LSQ has its search space of codebooks even larger than PQ, yet it has worse performance in most cases.

F.2. The Ablation of the Estimator

Recall that as is discussed in Section 3.2, unlike PQ which simply treats the quantized data vector as the data vector, our method explicitly analyzes the geometric relationship between the vectors and constructs an unbiased estimator accordingly. In this part, we ablate our estimator and adopt an alternative estimator ⟨𝐨¯,𝐪⟩\left<\mathbf{\bar{o}},\mathbf{q}\right> by treating the quantized data vector as the data vector as PQ does. In particular, we collect 10710^{7} pairs of the estimated inner products and the true inner products from the first 10 query vectors and the 10610^{6} data vectors of the GIST dataset. Figure 11 shows the scatter plots of the true inner product and the estimated inner product. The red points represent the results based our unbiased estimator ⟨𝐨¯,𝐪⟩⟨𝐨¯,𝐨⟩\frac{\left<\mathbf{\bar{o}},\mathbf{q}\right>}{\left<\mathbf{\bar{o}},\mathbf{o}\right>}. The blue points represent the results based on the estimator ⟨𝐨¯,𝐪⟩\left<\mathbf{\bar{o}},\mathbf{q}\right>. We fit the two set of points with linear regression. The results clearly show that our estimator is unbiased while the estimator ⟨𝐨¯,𝐪⟩\left<\mathbf{\bar{o}},\mathbf{q}\right> is biased by a ratio of around 0.8. Table 7 further presents the average relative error and maximum relative error of the estimated distances on the GIST dataset. It clearly shows that taking ⟨𝐨¯,𝐪⟩\left<\mathbf{\bar{o}},\mathbf{q}\right> as the estimator degrades both the general quality and the robustness of the distance estimation. Moreover, we note that based on the estimator ⟨𝐨¯,𝐪⟩\left<\mathbf{\bar{o}},\mathbf{q}\right>, the original theoretical error bound (Theorem 3.2) does not hold anymore. Thus, it is inapplicable for the error-bound-based re-ranking for in-memory ANN search (Section 4).

F.3. The Ablation of the Re-Ranking

As is discussed in Section 4, despite that RaBitQ provides the guarantee on the distance estimation, when the distances (to the query) of two different data vectors are extremely close to each other, the guaranteed accuracy might be insufficient for ranking them correctly. Re-ranking, in this case, is necessary for producing high recall. Figure 10 plots the “QPS”-“recall” curves of RaBitQ with and without re-ranking. It shows that re-ranking is indeed necessary for achieving the robust performance of ANN search.
